content: The contribution of hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) to the burden of disease varies significantly between countries, making it essential to tailor strategies at the national level. To address this, combined targets have been established for monitoring progress. For validation of elimination efforts, the proportion of individuals with chronic HBV who are receiving treatment and those with chronic HCV who have been cured are calculated based on the number of diagnosed cases. However, not all individuals diagnosed with chronic HBV are eligible for treatment, as eligibility criteria differ across countries and regions. These criteria should align with current World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines or relevant regional or national standards. Due to the high effectiveness of direct-acting antiviral drugs for HCV treatment, reporting the proportion of individuals achieving sustained viral response is not mandatory for elimination validation, though such data should be provided if available. Additionally, countries are encouraged to double their coverage of hepatitis-related interventions within a two-year period to accelerate progress. The WHO guidelines aim to simplify and integrate the collection, analysis, reporting, and use of strategic information on viral hepatitis at local, national, and global levels. These guidelines emphasize person-centered monitoring, prioritizing indicators that support prevention, diagnosis, and treatment interventions. They also provide stepwise guidance for building health information systems to strengthen hepatitis programs and improve data utilization. The guidelines are intended for national health sector staff involved in hepatitis-related data collection and analysis, as well as program managers, partner organizations, consultants, and researchers. They are relevant for health ministry decision-makers, health information system managers, and those working to improve hepatitis data quality. The WHO has also developed related documents, including global health sector strategies for HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (2022–2030), as well as technical reports on surveillance and monitoring for hepatitis B and C. These resources provide frameworks for planning, tracking progress, and improving surveillance systems. Key updates in the guidelines include an enhanced strategic information framework with 10 core global indicators for regular reporting, a focus on person-centered data monitoring, and recommendations for implementing surveillance systems tailored to different levels of country maturity. Hepatitis B and C infections can become chronic, leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Surveillance systems must address acute hepatitis, chronic infections, and their long-term complications. The clinical presentation of acute and chronic viral hepatitis is similar across all hepatitis viruses, and many infections are asymptomatic, making laboratory diagnosis essential for identifying the virus and differentiating between recent and chronic infections. The modes of transmission for hepatitis viruses vary. Hepatitis A and E are transmitted via the fecal-oral route, while hepatitis B and C are bloodborne. Hepatitis D requires co-infection with HBV. Surveillance approaches must be tailored to each country to include populations at higher risk of transmission and identify the predominant modes of transmission. Laboratory diagnosis is critical for surveillance, as it helps confirm the type of hepatitis virus and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Biomarker surveys are the gold standard for estimating the prevalence of chronic infections and guiding testing and treatment strategies. However, these surveys can be costly and should be integrated with other health-related population surveys to optimize resources. Surveillance of long-term complications, such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), is essential for evaluating the impact of prevention and treatment programs. Data from vital registration systems and clinical records can help estimate the fraction of these conditions attributable to hepatitis B and C. Combining data from multiple sources is necessary to fully understand a country’s epidemiological profile. The WHO has established standardized case definitions for acute and chronic hepatitis to improve surveillance and reporting. These definitions include clinical and biomarker criteria to differentiate between acute and chronic cases. Enhanced case reporting, which includes in vitro diagnosis and risk factor data collection, is recommended for acute hepatitis surveillance. The guidelines also provide a consolidated strategic information framework to monitor health sector responses to chronic hepatitis B and C. This framework includes a menu of indicators organized by priority and linked to a results chain, supporting high-quality care along the health sector cascade. Countries are encouraged to select and adapt indicators based on their context, priorities, and health system maturity.
